title: Why Your Students Don't Like You; And What To Do About It
author: Michael Linsin
summary: All students want to like their teacher, yet research shows most do not. The problem is not rooted in personality mismatch or inherent student dislike, but rather in how teachers approach relationships and structure classroom culture. Students like and respect teachers who demonstrate clear boundaries, follow through consistently on every promise, show genuine and visible care for their growth as people, and create an environment of safety and procedural fairness. Building positive student-teacher relationships requires intentional, deliberate effort to communicate reliability, consistency, and authentic interest in students as whole individuals—not merely as learners. Teachers must signal that they remember what matters to students, act predictably, and deliver on commitments. When these conditions are met, even initially reserved students warm to their teachers.
points: All students want to like their teacher, but most do not—this is a systemic problem rooted in teacher behavior, not student nature
Students like teachers who are consistent, reliable, and follow through on what they say they will do
Genuine care for student growth and individual wellbeing is foundational to positive relationships
Teachers who treat discipline and boundaries as expressions of care build stronger relationships than permissive teachers
Creating psychological safety and fairness in the classroom enables students to open up and engage meaningfully with the teacher
